stem: A liver transplant recipient with advanced liver disease develops rapid renal-function decline consistent with hepatorenal failure. Which management need aligns with standard complication references?

options.text: Renal replacement therapy is never indicated in hepatorenal failure
Immediate isolated kidney transplantation without liver evaluation
Permanent discontinuation of all transplant follow-up

explanation.rationale_correct: Hepatorenal failure involves rapid decrease in renal function in patients with advanced liver disease and may need to be treated with dialysis.

rationale_incorrect.B: Dialysis may be required when hepatorenal failure develops.
rationale_incorrect.C: Hepatorenal failure in advanced liver disease is evaluated in the context of liver transplantation rather than isolated kidney transplant alone.
rationale_incorrect.D: Hepatorenal failure requires ongoing transplant-team management rather than ending follow-up.

primary_anchor.quote_hint: Hepatorenal failure … rapid decrease in renal function … May need to be treated with dialysis

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 12 → hepatorenal failure → 6.c. (may require dialysis); PDF p. 643 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Source-first item. Hepatorenal-failure management angle paired with education item (cctc-1084); distinct from metabolic bone disease (cctc-3058); anchor verified on Cupples p. 643.

stem: A school-age pediatric transplant recipient develops slapped-cheek rash and severe anemia. Which infectious complication should the coordinator include in the differential?

options.text: Parvovirus B19 with possible pure red blood cell aplasia
Expected benign postoperative healing without infection evaluation
Oral aversion as the sole explanation for anemia
Hyperacute rejection presenting as slapped-cheek rash

explanation.rationale_correct: Parvovirus B19 is typically acquired during the school-age period and may cause a slapped-cheek rash with pure red blood cell aplasia and low hematocrit.

rationale_incorrect.B: Slapped-cheek rash with severe anemia warrants evaluation for infections such as parvovirus.
rationale_incorrect.C: Oral aversion is a feeding complication unrelated to parvovirus hematologic presentation.
rationale_incorrect.D: Hyperacute rejection does not present as slapped-cheek rash with aplastic anemia.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 5, Infectious Diseases → 4. Parvovirus B19 → a.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: school-age period … slapped cheek rash … pure red blood cell aplasia with low hematocrit

references.locator: Ch. 5 → 4. Parvovirus B19 → a. (school-age acquisition, slapped-cheek rash, red blood cell aplasia); PDF p. 208 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

stem: A coordinator is reviewing deceased-donor infection-prevention protocols with the procurement team. Evaluate the following statements about donor-transmitted infections:

elements.text: Donor-transmitted infection can cause significant recipient morbidity and mortality.
Unexpected donor-to-recipient infection transmission never occurs after transplantation.
Donor chart review is part of donor risk assessment.
Donor physical examination may reveal track marks suggesting recent drug use.

explanation.rationale_correct: Donor-transmitted infections may cause significant morbidity and mortality; donor chart review and physical examination including track marks are standard risk-assessment steps. Unexpected transmission can still occur, so statement II is false.

rationale_incorrect.A: Statement II is false; statements III and IV are also correct.
rationale_incorrect.C: Statement I is also true; statement II is false.
rationale_incorrect.D: Statement II is false—unexpected donor-to-recipient infection transmission remains an infrequent but recognized complication.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 5, Infectious Diseases → Donor-Transmitted Infections → A.–C.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: significant recipient morbidity and mortality … unexpected transmission … Donor chart review … track marks

references.citation: Core Curriculum for Transplant Nurses, 2nd ed. (Cupples et al., 2016).
references.locator: Ch. 5 → Donor-Transmitted Infections → A.–C. (morbidity/mortality risk, chart review, physical exam with track marks); PDF p. 181 (repo file-page index; printed margin may differ).

notes: Synthesized item. Twenty-fourth complex_combo in bank; donor-transmitted-infection angle distinct from BK risk combo (cctc-3076); anchor verified on Cupples p. 181.

stem: A heart transplant recipient more than one year post-transplant is being considered for calcineurin inhibitor (CNI) withdrawal with sirolimus. Which long-term benefit aligns with standard medication references?

options.text: Decreased allograft vasculopathy and improved long-term survival compared with continued CNI
Guaranteed elimination of all rejection risk without monitoring
Mandatory use in every heart recipient immediately after implantation
Complete avoidance of any immunosuppression after conversion

explanation.rationale_correct: Late conversion of CNI to sirolimus more than one year after heart transplantation has been associated with decreased allograft vasculopathy and improved long-term survival compared with continued CNI therapy.

rationale_incorrect.B: Immunosuppression conversion requires ongoing monitoring and does not eliminate all rejection risk.
rationale_incorrect.C: Sirolimus conversion is a selected late strategy rather than mandatory immediate therapy for every recipient.
rationale_incorrect.D: Sirolimus replaces CNI as maintenance immunosuppression rather than eliminating all immunosuppression.

primary_anchor.section: Ch. 4, Pharmacology → E. Proliferation Signal Inhibitors → 1.e.ii.
primary_anchor.quote_hint: late conversion (>1 year post heart transplantation) of CNI to sirolimus is associated with decreased allograft vasculopathy and improved long-term survival
